title: The routine gets tougher
description: Lookalike links, fake WhatsApp and SMS messages, and a USB stick someone found. Watch the details.

events.message: Several messages arrive at the same time! The clock is ticking.

emails.subject: You have a new message on WhatsApp Web
emails.bodyHtml: A new message has arrived on your WhatsApp Web. To view it, confirm your session by clicking the link below.

internalDbRecord.notes: No prior contact from this sender.

investigationHints.summaryText: WhatsApp doesn't notify you from an address like this. It's a random address, with no link to WhatsApp.
The link doesn't lead to the official WhatsApp Web (web.whatsapp.com), but to an unknown address.

explanation.short: Fake WhatsApp notification used to steal a login session.
explanation.detailed: WhatsApp never asks you to 'confirm your session' by email. The link does not go to web.whatsapp.com, and whoever sent it had never written to the company before — three signals that together leave no doubt.

emails.subject: Action required: temporarily disable your two-step verification
emails.bodyHtml: During our system migration, we ask that you temporarily turn off two-step verification on your account to avoid lockouts. Re-enable it after 24 hours.

aiAssistantHint.reasoning: Asking you to turn off two-step verification by email is a known scam. And the email's checks did not match.

investigationHints.summaryText: The address doesn't belong to the company or to any known IT vendor.
The automatic checks did not match: it did not come from who it claims.
The helper points to a high chance of a scam, and this time it is right.

explanation.short: A real IT team never asks you to turn off two-step verification.
explanation.detailed: Two-step verification is one of the best defenses against account takeover. A real IT team never asks you to turn it off by email — that removes exactly the protection that stops someone from using a leaked password. Add to that the address that isn't the official one.

emails.subject: I found a USB drive in the parking lot, is it yours?
emails.bodyHtml: Hi! I found a USB drive lying near the store entrance with a sticker showing initials similar to yours. I took photos of the contents before turning it in at the front desk — take a look at the attachment to see if it's yours.

internalDbRecord.notes: No employee with this name registered at Store 12.

investigationHints.summaryText: The '.zip' file is actually a Windows program, not photos.
In the sandbox, the file created a process with a name that mimics a system process (svhost32.exe, not svchost.exe).
No employee with that name is registered at the mentioned store.

explanation.short: Classic 'lost USB drive' bait adapted for email.
explanation.detailed: The 'lost USB drive' scam usually means leaving an infected drive in a public place for someone to plug in out of curiosity. Here the bait comes by email, in a file pretending to be photos. The 'zip' is actually a harmful program in disguise.

emails.subject: Registration open: information security training
emails.bodyHtml: Hello! Registration for this month's in-person information security training is now open. Spots are limited, sign up through the internal training system.

investigationHints.summaryText: The padlock is valid and was issued for the company's official address.

explanation.detailed: Official address, link to the real portal, no rush and no request for data. Every sign points to a real email.
